component_findings.manifest_constraints: Preserved paid evidence (ecosystem-tooling--part-1--java): When two dependencies require different versions of the same library, Maven resolves the conflict using the nearest-wins strategy: The version closest to your project in the dependency tree is chosen.

component_findings.registry_security: Preserved paid evidence (ecosystem-tooling--part-1--java): 0-100 score = equal-weighted average of four 0-25 component scores, applied identically to all 10 languages: (1) Availability of an official/de-facto-standard dependency manager with a declarative manifest format; (2) Central registry scale, reliability, and integrity guarantees (immutability, signing/verification requirements); (3) Dependency-resolution robustness: transitive resolution, version-conflict mediation, BOM/platform support, reproducibility/lock mechanisms; (4) Security/vulnerability tooling integration: availability of SCA tools and vulnerability databases integrated with the package manager.
component_findings.resolver_lock: Preserved paid evidence (ecosystem-tooling--part-1--java): Both Maven and Gradle support transitive dependency resolution and Bill-of-Materials/platform imports to align version sets across modules, and Gradle offers explicit resolutionStrategy overrides. A modest deduction reflects that Maven's default 'nearest-wins' transitive conflict strategy and the historical prevalence of classpath/diamond-dependency conflicts still require manual mediation (exclusions, forced versions) rather than being fully automatic or lockfile-guaranteed by default.
